**Direct answer:** No. WAL doesn't eliminate write contention. SQLite still allows only one writer at a time per database, in WAL mode as in rollback-journal mode. What WAL changes is that readers and the writer no longer block each other, and it also makes commits cheaper.

## Claims and sources

**Write contention remains**
- In WAL mode there is only one WAL file, so there can only be one writer at a time. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- SQLite supports many simultaneous read transactions but only one write transaction. https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html
- A writer that can't get the write lock gets SQLITE_BUSY. This is documented for rollback-journal mode (the RESERVED lock), and the one-writer rule holds in WAL as well. https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html and https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html
- Even `BEGIN CONCURRENT`, which allows multiple simultaneous writers, requires WAL or WAL2 mode and still serializes COMMITs. Conflicting commits fail with SQLITE_BUSY_SNAPSHOT. https://www.sqlite.org/src/doc/begin-concurrent/doc/begin_concurrent.md
- That page doesn't say whether `BEGIN CONCURRENT` is in the standard release. The "separate branch" description came from the fetch tool's background knowledge, not the page. I didn't verify it, so check your SQLite version.

**The real concurrency benefit**
- In WAL mode, readers don't block writers and a writer doesn't block readers, so reading and writing can proceed concurrently. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- The docs qualify this as "mostly true", and the exceptions are the SQLITE_BUSY cases below. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- In rollback-journal mode, a writer needs PENDING and then EXCLUSIVE locks to commit. While it waits, no new readers can start, and while it holds EXCLUSIVE, no readers can read. https://www.sqlite.org/lockingv3.html
- A reader keeps seeing a consistent historical snapshot while a writer modifies the database. https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html

**Other effects on throughput**
- WAL is "significantly faster in most scenarios". Commits write content once instead of twice, and the writes are sequential. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- WAL can be about 1–2% slower for read-mostly workloads that seldom write. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**Caveats and costs**
- Readers can still get SQLITE_BUSY in three cases: another connection holds the database in exclusive locking mode, the last connection is closing and cleaning up, or crash recovery is running. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- A checkpoint can't finish while any reader is active. If overlapping readers never leave a gap, the WAL file grows without bound. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- Read performance degrades as the WAL file grows, so regular checkpoints are needed. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- WAL doesn't work over network filesystems, because all processes must be on the same host. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- WAL doesn't give atomic commits across multiple ATTACHed databases. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
- Very large transactions were a problem before version 3.11.0 (2016). Since then WAL handles them as efficiently as rollback mode. https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**Practical handling of write contention**
- A deferred transaction that reads and then writes can fail with SQLITE_BUSY at the write if another connection has modified the database. `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` takes the write lock up front, so a failure happens before any work is done. https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html
- In WAL mode, EXCLUSIVE and IMMEDIATE transactions behave the same. https://www.sqlite.org/lang_transaction.html
- The busy-timeout claim is unsupported. The fetch tool said a busy timeout makes SQLite retry before returning SQLITE_BUSY. It also said the timeout doesn't apply to a blocked deferred read-to-write upgrade. Neither point was on the page, so I haven't established either.

## Limits of this research
I used four of the eight allowed retrievals, all on sqlite.org, so this is the official documentation's view. I didn't look at independent benchmarks of write throughput or at real-world contention behavior. Also, I researched this directly instead of spawning subagents and writing report files. The skill's folder setup needs shell commands, and you ruled those out.
